---
title: "Define interventions and future mortality"
description: "Apply explicit probability effects and extend patient simulations beyond fitted follow-up."
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(TrajectoryMarkovAnalysis)
invisible(capture.output(source(system.file(
  "examples", "quickstart.R", package = "TrajectoryMarkovAnalysis"
), local = TRUE)))
```

Effects and extrapolation are supplied modelling assumptions. Fitted counts do
not select an intervention effect, support cutoff or future mortality trend.
The short intervention example uses the synthetic
[quickstart objects](https://github.com/HealthInformaticsUT/TrajectoryMarkovAnalysis/blob/main/inst/examples/quickstart.R):

```{r load-example, eval=FALSE}
source(system.file("examples", "quickstart.R", package = "TrajectoryMarkovAnalysis"))
```

## Change a transition probability

```{r intervention}
effects <- list(prevention = list(
  from = "Stable", to = "Complication", multiplier = 0.75,
  redistributeTo = "Stable", startDay = 0, endDay = 28
))
treated <- projectCohort(
  transitions, nCycles = 4, initial = c(Stable = 1), cohortSize = 100,
  transitionEffects = effects
)
transitionMatrix(treated, cycle = 0)
```

The rule multiplies the selected destination probability and transfers the
exact difference to `redistributeTo`. For probabilities 0.70 Stable, 0.20
Complication and 0.10 Dead, the result is 0.75, 0.15 and 0.10. It is an effect
on discrete cycle probability, not a hazard ratio. Invalid rows cause an error.
Stored fitted matrices remain unchanged.

Windows use the **source** `elapsed_day`: start included, end excluded. In this
weekly example the rule covers sources at days 0, 7, 14 and 21. Simulation also
accepts `eligible = function(p) p$treatment_active`; its input is the current
source profile. Covariate updates affect the next draw. Projection has no
patient-level eligibility callback. Intervention fees are specified separately
through rewards or cost rules.

## Target stages or entry explicitly

For an ordered model, add `stage = "onset"` to change onset before mortality.
Omitting `stage` changes the combined cycle row and leaves intermediate paths
unavailable. Stage and net-cycle rules cannot be mixed. At most one applicable
rule may act on a source profile per stage, or per net step.

`applyAt = "transitions"` is the default. `"entry"` and `"both"` include a fitted
entry model explicitly. Entry and the first adjacent draw both have source day
zero: `applyAt = "both", endDay = 28` covers entry plus four weekly draws. For
four outcome labels, use an entry rule and an adjacent rule ending at day 21.
An entry fee can remain payable when entry produces death; it adds no baseline
cycle or living time. See the
[entry intervention example](https://github.com/HealthInformaticsUT/TrajectoryMarkovAnalysis/blob/main/inst/examples/entry-simulation.R).

## Switch to supplied later probabilities

`extendModelBundle()` attaches one explicit later model at `fromDay`. It must
share clinical states, absorbing states and cycle length; its groups and periods
can differ. Use your own `late_model` and source description:

```{r supplied-extension, eval=FALSE}
extended <- extendModelBundle(
  createModelBundle(transitions), fromDay = 364, transitions = late_model,
  source = "Description of the external evidence or assumption"
)
```

The step from day 357 to 364 uses the original model; the step from 364 to 371
uses the later model. Its period clock starts at the handover, while patient age,
treatment windows, cost periods and discounting keep their original clocks.
Entry and costs are not replaced. Unsupported later rows fail without falling
back to the original fit. Extensions operate in simulation and resumed runs,
not `projectCohort()`. See the
[runnable extension example](https://github.com/HealthInformaticsUT/TrajectoryMarkovAnalysis/blob/main/inst/examples/extrapolation-simulation.R).

## Supply background mortality

```{r background-mortality}
background <- createModelBundle(createMortalityTransitions(
  data.frame(death_probability = 0.02),
  states = c("Living", "Death"), deathState = "Death", cycleLength = 7,
  probabilityDays = 365.25, source = "Synthetic annual probability"
))
```

Supply probabilities rather than percentages or rates. An interval probability
`p` is converted to `1 - (1 - p)^(cycleLength / probabilityDays)`, assuming a
constant hazard over the supplied interval. The table can contain covariate
strata. This creates a mortality-only model; it does not automatically add
background mortality to an existing all-cause model.

## Calibrate excess and define the future tail

Use your study's matching histories, fitted bundle and background table. These
calls illustrate the connection; `study_histories` and `fitted_bundle` must come
from the same source-cycle support and use the named reference period.

```{r mortality-tail, eval=FALSE}
calibration <- calibrateExcessMortality(
  study_histories, background, deathStates = "Dead", periodLabels = "Observed"
)
future <- extrapolateMortality(
  fitted_bundle, calibration, fromDay = 364, referencePeriod = "Observed",
  excess = "linear", declineDays = 365.25,
  source = "Assumed excess hazard declines to zero over one year"
)
```

Calibration matches background to actual contributing observations. With observed
death probability `p`, mean matched background `b` and cycle days `c`, daily
excess is `(log(1 - b) - log(1 - p)) / c`. Negative excess needs an explicit
`negativeExcess = "zero"` policy; probability one needs an explicit finite
ceiling. Unsupported cells remain unavailable. A stage fit requires the named
mortality stage. Multiple death states need explicit `deathAllocation` for the tail.

The future model replaces mortality, preserving nondeath destination shares
conditional on survival. In a stage model only the mortality stage is replaced.
Constant excess keeps the calibrated daily hazard; linear excess integrates its
decline within each cycle. Current patient covariates select background and
excess, without interpolation or missing-group fallback. Use the complete
returned bundle with `simulateTrajectories()`; `projectCohort()` cannot use this
profile-dependent tail.

Run the full [future-mortality example](https://github.com/HealthInformaticsUT/TrajectoryMarkovAnalysis/blob/main/inst/examples/future-mortality-simulation.R)
for calendar ageing, audit fields and a reproducible resumed run. A shared seed
reproduces initialization; it does not guarantee paired draws across scenarios.
Continue with [cost and health outcomes](costs-and-economic-outcomes.html).
